circulose.origin: CIRCULOSE is a dissolving pulp made from discarded cotton textiles, not a fiber. It was developed by the Swedish company Renewcell, which was declared bankrupt in February 2024. Later in 2024 the private equity firm Altor acquired the business and its plant at Ortviken in Sundsvall, Sweden, and the company now operates under the name Circulose. The pulp is sold to fiber makers, who spin it into regenerated cellulose such as viscose; in 2025 Circulose announced a partnership with Jilin Chemical Fiber for viscose filament yarn.
circulose.structure: The product is a sheet of purified cellulose pulp, chemically cotton cellulose (beta-1,4-linked glucose) that has been shortened in chain length and cleaned to dissolving-pulp specifications. Dissolving pulps need high alpha-cellulose content, low hemicellulose and controlled viscosity (degree of polymerization) so that they react and dissolve evenly in viscose or lyocell processing. The fiber eventually made from CIRCULOSE takes the structure of whichever process is used, for example the cellulose II, skin-core morphology of viscose.
circulose.process: As the producer describes it, cotton-rich textile waste is sorted, shredded and cleaned of non-textile parts and non-cellulosic components; the material is then chemically treated to remove dyes and impurities and to adjust chain length, and the purified cellulose is formed into pulp sheets. These sheets are shipped to fiber producers, who dissolve them, often blended with wood pulp, and spin viscose, lyocell or other regenerated fibers. The producer describes CIRCULOSE as made entirely from discarded cotton textiles.
circulose.performance: Performance claims apply to the downstream fiber, not the pulp. A viscose made partly or fully from CIRCULOSE should behave like viscose: absorbent, soft, readily dyed with reactive and direct dyes, and much weaker when wet than dry. Whether recycled-cotton pulp changes spinning efficiency or fiber quality depends on the specific fiber producer's process and blend ratio, so buyers should rely on test reports for the actual fiber rather than on the pulp brand.
circulose.identify: Fibers containing CIRCULOSE cannot be distinguished from wood-based regenerated cellulose by burn tests (indicative only), microscopy or FTIR, because the polymer is the same. Identification depends on documentation from the pulp producer and fiber maker. A common error is listing CIRCULOSE as if it were the fiber on a garment; it is a feedstock inside a fiber that still needs its own generic name.
circulose.labeling: CIRCULOSE is a trademark for a pulp, not a generic fiber name. The finished fiber must be labeled by its generic name (for example rayon, viscose or lyocell) under the US TFPIA and 16 CFR Part 303 and under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Recycled-content claims need substantiation for the actual share present in the fiber and fabric. In late 2025 Circulose announced that its pulp would be available only to brands with direct partnerships, which affects how supply is documented.
circulose.past: Renewcell built a commercial-scale textile-to-pulp plant at Ortviken, Sundsvall, which the company describes as the first commercial-scale chemical textile recycling plant, but weak sales led to bankruptcy in February 2024. Altor bought the remaining assets later that year, renamed the business after its product, and left the plant idle while seeking volume commitments. In February 2026 Circulose announced, with commitments from 11 brands, that it planned to restart production in the fourth quarter of 2026. Whether production has resumed as of late 2026 should be checked with the company.

naia.origin: Naia is the cellulose acetate textile brand of Eastman Chemical Company, headquartered in Kingsport, Tennessee, where Eastman began commercial Naia production in 2017. The generic fiber is acetate: cellulose from wood pulp chemically esterified with acetyl groups. The range includes continuous filament yarn and, later, staple fiber. Naia Renew is a variant that Eastman describes as about 60% wood pulp and 40% certified recycled waste processed through its molecular recycling technology.
naia.structure: Acetate is a cellulose ester, not regenerated cellulose. In cellulose diacetate most, but not all, of the three hydroxyl groups on each anhydroglucose unit are replaced by acetyl ester groups, which removes much of the hydrogen bonding that makes cellulose insoluble and hydrophilic. The result is a thermoplastic, acetone-soluble polymer with lower moisture uptake than viscose. Dry-spun acetate filaments typically have a lobed or crenulated cross-section formed as solvent leaves the filament surface, contributing to acetate's characteristic luster.
naia.process: In the conventional acetate route that Naia follows, wood pulp is acetylated with acetic acid and acetic anhydride to form cellulose acetate, which is partly hydrolyzed to the diacetate and made into flake. The flake is dissolved in acetone to make a spinning dope, which is extruded through spinnerets into warm air where the acetone evaporates (dry spinning, without a water bath). Eastman states that the acetone and acetic acid are recovered and recycled in a closed loop. For Naia Renew, Eastman states that plastic waste is broken down to molecular building blocks that feed acetyl production.
naia.performance: Acetate has moderate moisture regain, lower than viscose but far above polyester, and modest strength that falls when wet. It is thermoplastic: it softens and can glaze at ironing temperatures and dissolves in acetone and some nail-polish removers. It is dyed with disperse dyes because acetylation removes the hydroxyl sites that reactive and direct dyes need. Eastman describes Naia as silky, breathable and, in staple form, reduced in pilling, and states that Naia Renew has a carbon footprint about 35% lower than standard Naia; these are producer claims.
naia.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: acetate burns and melts, dripping, with an acrid vinegar-like odor and a hard, irregular bead. A classic solubility check is that acetate dissolves in acetone while triacetate, viscose and cotton do not. FTIR shows ester carbonyl absorption that separates acetate from regenerated cellulose. Acetate is sometimes confused with viscose or described as silk in retail copy.
naia.labeling: Naia is a trademark, not a generic name. US labels must use acetate (or triacetate where applicable) under the TFPIA and 16 CFR Part 303, and EU labels acetate under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Eastman states that the recycled waste in Naia Renew is certified under the Global Recycled Standard (GRS); buyers should ask how the recycled share is measured or allocated and which certificate covers the specific product.
naia.past: Cellulose acetate became a commercial artificial-silk fiber in the early twentieth century, and Eastman developed Naia from its long-established cellulosics business. It launched the reformulated Naia textile yarn in January 2017 and started commercial-scale production at Kingsport that year. It added staple fiber for knits and blends, then Naia Renew with recycled content from its carbon renewal (molecular recycling) technology, and later filament variants shown at trade fairs such as Intertextile Shanghai in 2025.
facts: about 60% wood pulp, 40% certified recycled waste
